subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Great London Smog
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Great London Smog usable.

hook.text: In December 1952, a thick yellow fog settled over London and refused to leave for five days.

buildup.text: Cold weather trapped coal smoke at ground level. Visibility dropped to near zero.

discovery.text: Hospitals overflowed. Undertakers ran out of coffins. An estimated 12,000 people died.

twist.text: The government initially blamed influenza. It took years to admit coal smoke was the killer.

climax.text: The disaster led to the Clean Air Act of 1956 — the world's first major air quality law.

punchline.text: London's deadliest disaster wasn't a bomb. It was the air.

quiz.question: How many people died in the 1952 Great London Smog?

details.summary: The Great London Smog of December 1952 killed an estimated 12,000 people when cold, windless weather trapped coal smoke over the city for five days. The disaster directly led to the UK Clean Air Act of 1956, one of the world's first air-pollution laws.
details.whyItMatters: The London smog is the most cited example of how pollution catastrophes drive policy change. It proved that clean-air regulation could prevent mass casualties.
takeaways: Coal smoke combined with fog to create a lethal sulfurous smog
Hospitals overflowed and visibility dropped to near zero for days
The resulting Clean Air Act banned coal burning in urban zones

faq.question: How many people did the Great London Smog kill?
faq.answer: Initial estimates cited 4,000 deaths, but later research using extended mortality data raised the toll to roughly 12,000. Most victims were elderly or already suffering from respiratory and cardiovascular conditions.

faq.question: What specific pollutant made the 1952 smog so deadly?
faq.answer: Sulfur dioxide from coal combustion combined with soot particles and fog droplets to form sulfuric acid aerosol. This acidic mist penetrated deep into lungs, causing acute bronchitis, pneumonia, and heart failure.
